<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
<meta charset="UTF-8">
<title>JavaScript — Interview Prep</title>
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com">
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin>
<link href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Atkinson+Hyperlegible+Next:ital,wght@0,400;0,500;0,700;1,400&family=Bricolage+Grotesque:opsz,wght@12..96,500..800&family=IBM+Plex+Mono:wght@400;500;600&display=swap" rel="stylesheet">
<style>
  /* study-theme v4 "whiteboard": the one stylesheet every guide uses. Edit here, then run
     `npm run study:upgrade` to apply it to every guide (lib.upgrade swaps each guide's <style> for this file).
     Token names are also used inside the SVG diagrams (dg*.mjs), so rename none of them. */
  :root{
    /* light: a whiteboard. Navy ink, blue marker for actions, green for done, yellow highlighter. */
    --bg:#F5F7FA;
    --panel:#FFFFFF;
    --panel-2:#EEF2F7;
    --border:#D3DAE5;
    --text:#14213D;
    --muted:#4F5D78;
    --accent:#1B55C5;
    --accent-ink:#FFFFFF;
    --accent-soft:#E4EDFC;
    --gold:#7A5200;
    --gold-soft:#FFF1B8;
    --ok:#126B4B;
    --ok-soft:#DDF3E9;
    --code-bg:#EEF2F7;
    --danger:#B42318;
    --shadow: 0 1px 2px rgba(20,33,61,.06), 0 4px 14px rgba(20,33,61,.04);
    --mono: 'IBM Plex Mono', ui-monospace, SFMono-Regular, Menlo, Consolas, monospace;
    --sans: 'Atkinson Hyperlegible Next', 'Atkinson Hyperlegible', -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', sans-serif;
    --display: 'Bricolage Grotesque', var(--sans);
    --measure: 76ch;
  }
  @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark){
    :root:not([data-theme="light"]){
      /* dark: a chalkboard. Chalk white text, chalk blue / yellow / green accents. */
      --bg:#101A19;
      --panel:#17231F;
      --panel-2:#1E2D29;
      --border:#33493F;
      --text:#ECF1EE;
      --muted:#A9B8B1;
      --accent:#93BCFF;
      --accent-ink:#0A1730;
      --accent-soft:#1D3048;
      --gold:#F0CF6B;
      --gold-soft:#3A3216;
      --ok:#7FD6A8;
      --ok-soft:#173327;
      --code-bg:#0C1513;
      --danger:#F5A99C;
      --shadow: 0 1px 2px rgba(0,0,0,.4);
    }
  }
  :root[data-theme="dark"]{
    --bg:#101A19;
    --panel:#17231F;
    --panel-2:#1E2D29;
    --border:#33493F;
    --text:#ECF1EE;
    --muted:#A9B8B1;
    --accent:#93BCFF;
    --accent-ink:#0A1730;
    --accent-soft:#1D3048;
    --gold:#F0CF6B;
    --gold-soft:#3A3216;
    --ok:#7FD6A8;
    --ok-soft:#173327;
    --code-bg:#0C1513;
    --danger:#F5A99C;
    --shadow: 0 1px 2px rgba(0,0,0,.4);
  }

  *{box-sizing:border-box;}
  html,body{margin:0;padding:0;}
  html{color-scheme:light dark; scroll-padding-top:16px;}
  body{
    background:var(--bg);
    color:var(--text);
    font-family:var(--sans);
    font-size:16px;
    line-height:1.6;
    -webkit-font-smoothing:antialiased;
    text-rendering:optimizeLegibility;
  }
  a{color:var(--accent); text-underline-offset:2px;}
  :focus-visible{outline:2px solid var(--accent); outline-offset:2px; border-radius:4px;}
  ::selection{background:var(--gold-soft); color:var(--text);}

  .app{display:flex; min-height:100vh;}

  /* ---------- Sidebar ---------- */
  .sidebar{
    width:288px;
    flex:0 0 288px;
    border-right:1px solid var(--border);
    background:var(--panel);
    padding:18px 14px 24px;
    position:sticky;
    top:0;
    height:100vh;
    overflow-y:auto;
    scrollbar-width:thin;
  }
  .side-top{display:flex; align-items:center; justify-content:space-between; gap:8px; margin:0 0 14px;}
  .home-link{display:inline-flex; align-items:center; gap:6px; font-size:14px; font-weight:500; color:var(--muted); text-decoration:none; padding:6px 8px; border-radius:8px;}
  .home-link:hover{color:var(--accent); background:var(--accent-soft);}
  .theme-btn{font:inherit; font-size:15px; line-height:1; width:34px; height:34px; color:var(--muted); background:transparent; border:1px solid var(--border); border-radius:8px; cursor:pointer;}
  .theme-btn:hover{color:var(--accent); border-color:var(--accent);}
  .brand{
    font-size:13.5px;
    line-height:1.45;
    color:var(--muted);
    padding:0 8px 16px;
    border-bottom:1px solid var(--border);
    margin-bottom:14px;
  }
  .brand b{display:block; font-family:var(--display); font-size:19px; font-weight:700; letter-spacing:-0.01em; color:var(--text);}
  .brand br{display:none;}
  .nav-item{
    display:flex;
    align-items:center;
    justify-content:space-between;
    gap:10px;
    width:100%;
    text-align:left;
    padding:9px 10px;
    border-radius:9px;
    border:1px solid transparent;
    background:transparent;
    color:var(--text);
    font-family:var(--sans);
    font-size:15px;
    line-height:1.35;
    cursor:pointer;
    margin-bottom:2px;
  }
  .nav-item:hover{background:var(--panel-2);}
  .nav-item.active{background:var(--accent-soft); color:var(--text); font-weight:700; box-shadow:inset 3px 0 0 var(--accent);}
  .nav-num{font-size:12.5px; font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums; color:var(--muted); width:20px; flex:0 0 20px;}
  .nav-item.active .nav-num{color:var(--accent);}
  .nav-label{flex:1;}
  .nav-count{
    font-size:12px;
    font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums;
    color:var(--muted);
    background:var(--panel-2);
    border:1px solid var(--border);
    padding:1px 7px;
    border-radius:999px;
  }
  .nav-item.complete .nav-count{color:var(--ok); border-color:var(--ok); background:var(--ok-soft);}
  .progress-box{
    margin-top:20px;
    padding:14px 12px;
    border:1px solid var(--border);
    border-radius:12px;
    background:var(--panel-2);
  }
  .progress-box .label{font-size:12.5px; font-weight:700; color:var(--muted); margin-bottom:8px; text-transform:lowercase;}
  .progress-box .label::first-letter{text-transform:uppercase;}
  .progress-track{height:8px; border-radius:999px; background:var(--border); overflow:hidden;}
  .progress-fill{height:100%; background:var(--ok); width:0%; transition:width .25s ease;}
  .progress-num{margin-top:8px; font-size:13.5px; font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums; color:var(--text);}
  .reset-btn{
    margin-top:10px;
    width:100%;
    font-family:var(--sans);
    font-size:13px;
    color:var(--muted);
    background:transparent;
    border:1px solid var(--border);
    border-radius:8px;
    padding:7px 8px;
    cursor:pointer;
  }
  .reset-btn:hover{color:var(--danger);border-color:var(--danger);}

  /* ---------- Main ---------- */
  .main{
    flex:1;
    min-width:0;
    padding:40px 48px 96px;
    max-width:1080px;
  }
  .hero{margin-bottom:36px;}
  .hero .eyebrow-free{display:none;}
  .hero h1{
    font-family:var(--display);
    font-size:clamp(28px, 3.4vw, 40px);
    line-height:1.12;
    margin:0 0 14px;
    font-weight:700;
    letter-spacing:-0.02em;
    text-wrap:balance;
  }
  .hero p{color:var(--muted); max-width:68ch; margin:0 0 6px; font-size:16.5px;}
  .hero p strong{color:var(--text);}
  .hero .source-note{font-size:13.5px; color:var(--muted); margin-top:18px; line-height:1.9;}

  .section-head{
    display:flex;
    align-items:baseline;
    gap:12px;
    margin:44px 0 14px;
    padding-bottom:12px;
    border-bottom:2px solid var(--text);
  }
  .section-head .num{font-family:var(--display); color:var(--accent); font-size:17px; font-weight:700; font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums;}
  .section-head h2{font-family:var(--display); font-size:26px; line-height:1.2; margin:0; font-weight:700; letter-spacing:-0.015em;}
  .section-head .count{margin-left:auto; font-size:13.5px; font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums; color:var(--muted); white-space:nowrap;}

  .qcard{
    border:1px solid var(--border);
    border-radius:14px;
    background:var(--panel);
    margin-bottom:10px;
    overflow:hidden;
    box-shadow:var(--shadow);
  }
  .qcard:hover{border-color:var(--accent);}
  .qcard.open{border-color:var(--accent); box-shadow:inset 4px 0 0 var(--accent), var(--shadow);}
  .qcard.focused{outline:2px solid var(--accent); outline-offset:1px;}
  .qhead{
    display:flex;
    align-items:flex-start;
    gap:14px;
    padding:15px 18px;
    cursor:pointer;
    user-select:none;
  }
  .qcheck{
    margin-top:3px;
    flex:0 0 auto;
    width:20px;height:20px;
    border-radius:6px;
    border:1.5px solid var(--muted);
    display:flex;align-items:center;justify-content:center;
    cursor:pointer;
    background:var(--panel);
  }
  .qcheck:hover{border-color:var(--ok);}
  .qcheck.done{background:var(--ok); border-color:var(--ok);}
  .qcheck.done::after{content:"✓"; color:var(--panel); font-size:13px; font-weight:700;}
  .qmain{flex:1; min-width:0; display:flex; flex-direction:column; gap:5px;}
  .qtext{flex:1; font-size:16.5px; line-height:1.4; font-weight:700;}
  .qtext.done-text{color:var(--muted); font-weight:500;}
  .qchips{display:flex; gap:6px; flex-wrap:wrap;}
  .qsec,.qcore{font-size:12px; padding:1px 8px; border-radius:99px; border:1px solid var(--border); color:var(--muted); background:var(--panel-2);}
  .qcore{color:var(--gold); border-color:var(--gold); background:var(--gold-soft);}
  .qsum{font-size:14.5px; color:var(--muted); line-height:1.5; max-width:var(--measure);}
  .qcard.open .qsum{display:none;}
  .qchevron{
    flex:0 0 auto;
    color:var(--muted);
    font-size:20px;
    line-height:1;
    transform:rotate(0deg);
    transition:transform .15s ease;
    margin-top:2px;
  }
  .qcard.open .qchevron{transform:rotate(90deg); color:var(--accent);}
  .qbody{
    display:none;
    padding:2px 22px 22px 52px;
    border-top:1px solid var(--border);
    font-size:16px;
    line-height:1.65;
  }
  .qcard.open .qbody{display:block; padding-top:18px;}
  /* Prose keeps a readable line length; tables, code and diagrams may use the full card width. */
  .qbody > p, .qbody > ul, .qbody > ol, .qbody > blockquote, .qbody > .callout, .qbody > h3, .qbody > h4{max-width:var(--measure);}
  .qbody p{margin:0 0 14px;}
  .qbody ul, .qbody ol{margin:0 0 14px; padding-left:22px;}
  .qbody li{margin-bottom:7px;}
  .qbody li::marker{color:var(--accent);}
  .qbody strong{color:var(--text); font-weight:700;}
  .qbody h3, .qbody h4{font-family:var(--display); font-size:17px; margin:20px 0 8px; letter-spacing:-0.01em;}
  code{
    font-family:var(--mono);
    background:var(--code-bg);
    border:1px solid var(--border);
    padding:0 5px;
    border-radius:5px;
    font-size:0.875em;
    overflow-wrap:anywhere;
  }
  pre{
    font-family:var(--mono);
    background:var(--code-bg);
    color:var(--text);
    padding:14px 16px;
    border-radius:10px;
    overflow-x:auto;
    font-size:13.5px;
    line-height:1.65;
    margin:0 0 16px;
    border:1px solid var(--border);
    tab-size:2;
  }
  pre code{background:none; border:0; padding:0; font-size:inherit;}
  /* syntax colouring added by the engine (comments, strings, keywords, numbers) */
  .tk-c{color:var(--muted); font-style:italic;}
  .tk-s{color:var(--ok);}
  .tk-k{color:var(--accent); font-weight:500;}
  .tk-n{color:var(--gold);}
  .diagram{
    background:var(--panel-2);
    border:1px solid var(--border);
    border-radius:12px;
    padding:16px;
    margin:0 0 16px;
    overflow-x:auto;
  }
  .diagram svg{display:block; margin:0 auto; max-width:100%; height:auto;}
  .diagram.lightbg{background:#F8FAFC; border-color:#CBD5E1;}
  .diagram.lightbg .codelabel{color:#334155;}
  .tag{
    display:inline-block;
    font-size:12px;
    color:var(--gold);
    background:var(--gold-soft);
    border:1px solid var(--gold);
    border-radius:6px;
    padding:1px 7px;
    margin-bottom:10px;
  }
  .tscroll{overflow-x:auto; margin:0 0 16px;}
  .tscroll > table.cmp{margin:0;}
  table.cmp{
    width:100%;
    border-collapse:collapse;
    margin:0 0 16px;
    font-size:14.5px;
    line-height:1.5;
  }
  table.cmp th, table.cmp td{
    border:1px solid var(--border);
    padding:9px 12px;
    text-align:left;
    vertical-align:top;
  }
  table.cmp th{background:var(--panel-2); font-size:13.5px; font-weight:700;}
  table.cmp tr:nth-child(odd) td{background:color-mix(in srgb, var(--panel-2) 45%, transparent);}

  .tbadge{display:inline-block; font-size:12px; font-weight:700; color:var(--gold); background:var(--gold-soft); border:1px solid var(--gold); border-radius:99px; padding:2px 10px; margin-bottom:10px;}
  .deeper{margin-top:16px; padding-top:12px; border-top:1px dashed var(--border); font-size:14.5px; line-height:1.9;}
  .deeper + .deeper{margin-top:2px; padding-top:0; border-top:0;}
  a.go{color:var(--accent); text-decoration:none; border-bottom:1px solid color-mix(in srgb, var(--accent) 35%, transparent);}
  a.go:hover{border-bottom-color:var(--accent);}

  .search{width:100%; box-sizing:border-box; margin:0 0 14px; padding:10px 12px; font:inherit; font-size:14.5px; color:var(--text); background:var(--bg); border:1px solid var(--border); border-radius:10px;}
  .search::placeholder{color:var(--muted);}
  .search:focus{outline:2px solid var(--accent); outline-offset:1px;}
  .qcheck:focus-visible{outline:2px solid var(--accent); outline-offset:2px;}
  mark{background:var(--gold-soft); color:var(--text); border-radius:3px; padding:0 2px;}
  .toolbar{display:flex; flex-wrap:wrap; align-items:center; gap:10px 16px; margin:0 0 18px; font-size:14px; color:var(--muted);}
  .toolbar .tmeta{font-size:13.5px; margin-right:auto;}
  .toolbar .tgroup{display:flex; gap:10px; align-items:center; flex-wrap:wrap;}
  .toolbar button{font:inherit; font-size:13.5px; color:var(--text); background:var(--panel); border:1px solid var(--border); border-radius:8px; padding:6px 12px; cursor:pointer;}
  .toolbar button:hover{border-color:var(--accent); color:var(--accent);}
  .toolbar label{display:flex; gap:6px; align-items:center; cursor:pointer; white-space:nowrap;}
  .toolbar input{accent-color:var(--accent); width:15px; height:15px;}
  .empty{color:var(--muted); font-size:15px; padding:18px; border:1px dashed var(--border); border-radius:12px;}
  .pager{display:flex; justify-content:space-between; gap:12px; margin-top:28px;}
  .pager button{font:inherit; font-size:14.5px; font-weight:500; color:var(--accent); background:var(--panel); border:1px solid var(--border); border-radius:10px; padding:12px 16px; cursor:pointer; max-width:48%; text-align:left;}
  .pager button:last-child{text-align:right;}
  .pager button:hover{border-color:var(--accent); background:var(--accent-soft);}
  .back-btn{position:fixed; right:22px; bottom:22px; z-index:10; font:inherit; font-size:14px; font-weight:700; color:var(--accent-ink); background:var(--accent); border:0; border-radius:99px; padding:11px 18px; cursor:pointer; box-shadow:0 6px 18px rgba(0,0,0,.22);}
  .keys{display:inline-block; margin-top:6px;}
  kbd{font-family:var(--mono); font-size:11.5px; padding:0 5px; border:1px solid var(--border); border-bottom-width:2px; border-radius:5px; background:var(--panel); color:var(--text);}
  .hero-actions{margin-top:18px; display:flex; flex-wrap:wrap; gap:10px;}
  .fc-start,.toolbar .flash-btn{font:inherit; font-weight:700; color:var(--accent-ink); background:var(--accent); border:1px solid var(--accent); border-radius:10px; cursor:pointer;}
  .fc-start{font-size:15px; padding:10px 18px;}
  .toolbar .flash-btn{color:var(--accent-ink);}
  .toolbar .flash-btn:hover{color:var(--accent-ink);}
  .fc-start:hover,.toolbar .flash-btn:hover{filter:brightness(1.1);}
  button.fc-start.alt{background:var(--panel); color:var(--accent); border:1px solid var(--accent);}
  button.fc-start.alt:hover{background:var(--accent-soft); filter:none;}
  a.fc-start.alt{display:inline-block; text-decoration:none; background:var(--panel); color:var(--accent); border:1px solid var(--accent);}

  /* ---------- Flashcards ---------- */
  body.fc-lock{overflow:hidden;}
  .fc{position:fixed; inset:0; z-index:50; background:rgba(8,14,26,.6); display:flex; align-items:center; justify-content:center; padding:24px;}
  .fc[hidden]{display:none;}
  .fc-dialog{width:min(920px,100%); max-height:100%; display:flex; flex-direction:column; background:var(--panel); border:1px solid var(--border); border-radius:18px; box-shadow:0 24px 70px rgba(0,0,0,.4); outline:none;}
  .fc-head{display:flex; justify-content:space-between; align-items:flex-start; gap:12px; padding:18px 22px 12px;}
  .fc-title{font-family:var(--display); font-size:17px; font-weight:700;}
  .fc-count{font-size:13px; font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums; color:var(--muted); margin-top:3px;}
  .fc-tools{display:flex; gap:12px; align-items:center; font-size:14px; color:var(--muted);}
  .fc-tools label{display:flex; gap:6px; align-items:center; cursor:pointer;}
  .fc-tools input{accent-color:var(--accent);}
  .fc-tools button{font:inherit; font-size:15px; color:var(--muted); background:transparent; border:1px solid var(--border); border-radius:8px; width:34px; height:34px; cursor:pointer;}
  .fc-bar{height:5px; background:var(--border); margin:0 22px; border-radius:99px; overflow:hidden;}
  .fc-bar i{display:block; height:100%; width:0; background:var(--ok); transition:width .2s ease;}
  .fc-body{flex:1; overflow-y:auto; padding:24px 26px; min-height:220px;}
  .fc-q{font-family:var(--display); font-size:25px; line-height:1.3; margin:12px 0 18px; font-weight:700; letter-spacing:-0.015em; text-wrap:balance;}
  .fc-prompt{color:var(--muted); font-size:15px; border:1px dashed var(--border); border-radius:12px; padding:28px 18px; text-align:center;}
  .fc .qbody.fc-a{display:block; border-top:1px solid var(--border); padding:18px 0 0; font-size:16px;}
  .fc-done h3{font-family:var(--display); font-size:22px; margin:0 0 8px;}
  .fc-done .fc-sub{color:var(--muted); margin:14px 0 6px;}
  .fc-done ul{padding-left:20px; font-size:15px;}
  .fc-actions{display:flex; gap:10px; justify-content:flex-end; padding:14px 22px; border-top:1px solid var(--border); flex-wrap:wrap;}
  .fc-actions button{font:inherit; font-size:15px; color:var(--text); background:var(--panel); border:1px solid var(--border); border-radius:10px; padding:10px 18px; cursor:pointer;}
  .fc-actions button.primary{color:var(--accent-ink); background:var(--accent); border-color:var(--accent); font-weight:700;}
  .fc-actions button.again{border-color:var(--gold); color:var(--gold);}
  .fc-actions button:first-child{margin-right:auto;}
  .fc-actions kbd{margin-left:6px; background:transparent; border-color:currentColor; color:inherit; opacity:.8;}
  .fc-keys{font-size:12.5px; color:var(--muted); padding:0 22px 16px; text-align:right;}

  /* ---------- Answer building blocks ---------- */
  .lede{font-size:17px; color:var(--text); font-weight:500;}
  .callout{background:var(--accent-soft); border:1px solid color-mix(in srgb, var(--accent) 45%, transparent); border-left:4px solid var(--accent); border-radius:10px; padding:12px 16px; margin:0 0 16px;}
  .callout.warning{background:var(--gold-soft); border-color:var(--gold);}
  .callout > :last-child{margin-bottom:0;}
  .note{font-size:14px; color:var(--muted);}
  .codelabel{font-size:13px; font-weight:700; color:var(--accent); margin:12px 0 5px;}
  .verified{font-size:13.5px; color:var(--muted); border-top:1px dashed var(--border); padding-top:8px; margin-top:12px;}
  .verified strong{color:var(--accent);}
  .keyline{font-family:var(--mono); font-size:13px; color:var(--accent);}
  .followup{border-left:3px solid var(--gold); padding-left:12px; color:var(--text);}
  .gcards{display:grid; grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fit,minmax(260px,1fr)); gap:12px; margin:0 0 16px;}
  .gcard{border:1px solid var(--border); border-radius:12px; background:var(--panel-2); padding:14px 16px;}
  .gcard h3,.gcard h4{margin:0 0 6px; font-size:15px; font-family:var(--sans);}
  .gcard ul{margin:0; padding-left:18px;}
  .rail{display:flex; flex-wrap:wrap; align-items:center; gap:6px; margin:0 0 16px; font-size:14px;}
  .rail span{background:var(--panel-2); border:1px solid var(--border); border-radius:8px; padding:6px 10px;}
  .rail span b{display:block; font-size:11.5px; color:var(--accent);}

{
  id:"js-scope", title:"Scope & Closures",
  questions:[
    {
      q:"How do closures work in JavaScript, and where are they used?",
      a:`<p>A closure is what you get when a function "remembers" the variables from the scope it was created in, even after that outer scope has finished running. JavaScript functions don't just carry their code — they carry a reference to the environment they were defined in.</p>
      <div class="diagram"><svg viewBox="0 0 560 190" width="560">
    <rect x="20" y="20" width="520" height="150" rx="10" fill="none" stroke="var(--border)" stroke-width="1.5"/>
    <text x="34" y="42" font-family="var(--mono)" font-size="12" fill="var(--muted)">function outer() {</text>
    <rect x="45" y="55" width="470" height="95" rx="8" fill="var(--accent-soft)" stroke="var(--accent)" stroke-width="1.5"/>
    <text x="58" y="76" font-family="var(--mono)" font-size="12" fill="var(--text)">let count = 0;   // captured variable</text>
    <text x="58" y="98" font-family="var(--mono)" font-size="12" fill="var(--text)">function inner() { count++; return count; }</text>
    <text x="58" y="120" font-family="var(--mono)" font-size="12" fill="var(--text)">return inner;    // keeps a link to this scope</text>
    <text x="34" y="164" font-family="var(--mono)" font-size="12" fill="var(--muted)">}</text>
    <text x="270" y="15" font-family="var(--mono)" font-size="11" fill="var(--gold)" text-anchor="middle">outer() has already returned — "count" is still alive</text>
  </svg></div>
      <p>Classic uses: private state before ES6 classes existed (a counter that only exposes <code>increment()</code> and <code>getValue()</code>, with the actual number hidden), factory functions that pre-configure behavior, and memoization/caching functions.</p>
      <p><strong>Good interview signal:</strong> the candidate mentions that closures capture the <em>variable</em>, not a snapshot of its value at creation time — this is what trips people up in loop + <code>setTimeout</code> examples.</p>
      <p><strong>Common follow-ups</strong></p>
      <ul>
        <li><strong>Give a concrete use case.</strong> A private counter: <code>createCounter()</code> returns <code>{ increment, get }</code>, closing over a <code>count</code> variable that nothing outside the function can reach directly.</li>
        <li><strong>How do closures cause React bugs?</strong> A callback or effect that closes over a prop/state value from an earlier render keeps using that stale value if it's missing from the dependency array — the classic "why does my handler still see the old count" bug.</li>
      </ul>`
    },
    {
      q:"What's the classic var vs let closure bug in a loop, and how do you fix it?",
      a:`<p>This is one of the most common closure gotchas in interviews. With <code>var</code>, every iteration of a loop shares the <em>same</em> variable, because <code>var</code> is function-scoped, not block-scoped. By the time an async callback actually runs, the loop has already finished, so every callback sees the final value.</p>
      <pre>for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 1000);
}
// logs 3, 3, 3 — every closure shares one 'i'</pre>
      <p>Switching to <code>let</code> fixes it because <code>let</code> is block-scoped: each iteration of the loop gets its own fresh binding, so each closure captures a different <code>i</code>.</p>
      <pre>for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 1000);
}
// logs 0, 1, 2 — a new 'i' binding per iteration</pre>
      <p><strong>Common follow-ups</strong></p>
      <ul>
        <li><strong>How would you fix it without <code>let</code>?</strong> Wrap the loop body in an IIFE that takes <code>i</code> as a parameter, creating a new scope per iteration — the pre-ES6 fix.</li>
        <li><strong>Does this affect <code>forEach</code>?</strong> No — <code>forEach</code>'s callback creates a new function scope on every call regardless of <code>var</code>/<code>let</code>, so this bug is specific to classic <code>for</code> loops.</li>
      </ul>`
    },
    {
      q:"What is the difference between var, let, and const?",
      a:`<table class="cmp">
<tr><th></th><th><code>var</code></th><th><code>let</code></th><th><code>const</code></th></tr>
<tr><td>Scope</td><td>Function</td><td>Block</td><td>Block</td></tr>
<tr><td>Hoisting</td><td>Hoisted and initialised to <code>undefined</code></td><td>Hoisted but in the temporal dead zone until declared</td><td>Same as <code>let</code></td></tr>
<tr><td>Reassign</td><td>Yes</td><td>Yes</td><td>No (binding is fixed)</td></tr>
<tr><td>Redeclare in same scope</td><td>Yes</td><td>No</td><td>No</td></tr>
<tr><td>Global object property</td><td>Yes (at top level of a script)</td><td>No</td><td>No</td></tr>
</table>
<ul>
<li><strong><code>const</code> is not immutability.</strong> It prevents reassigning the binding, but an object or array it points to can still be mutated. Use <code>Object.freeze</code> (shallow) or immutable updates when you need more.</li>
<li><strong>Temporal dead zone:</strong> reading a <code>let</code>/<code>const</code> before its declaration throws a <code>ReferenceError</code> instead of silently giving <code>undefined</code>.</li>
<li><strong>Loop closures:</strong> <code>let</code> in a <code>for</code> loop creates a fresh binding per iteration, which fixes the classic <code>var</code> bug (see the closure-in-a-loop question).</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>Interview tip:</strong> default to <code>const</code>, use <code>let</code> only when you reassign, and avoid <code>var</code>.</p>`
    },
    {
      q:"What are hoisting and the temporal dead zone?",
      a:`<p class="lede">Before running a scope, JavaScript creates its bindings. That is <em>hoisting</em>: declarations are known before their line runs, but what you can do with them before that line differs by kind.</p><table class="cmp"><tr><th>Declaration</th><th>Hoisted?</th><th>Before its line</th></tr><tr><td><code>var</code></td><td>yes, initialized to <code>undefined</code></td><td>reads give <code>undefined</code></td></tr><tr><td><code>let</code> / <code>const</code></td><td>yes, but <strong>uninitialized</strong></td><td>throws <code>ReferenceError</code> (the temporal dead zone)</td></tr><tr><td><code>function foo() {}</code></td><td>yes, fully (name and body)</td><td>can be called early</td></tr><tr><td><code>const foo = () => {}</code> / <code>var foo = function(){}</code></td><td>only the variable</td><td>TypeError / ReferenceError when called early</td></tr><tr><td><code>class Foo {}</code></td><td>like <code>let</code></td><td>ReferenceError</td></tr></table><pre>console.log(a);   // undefined   (var is hoisted and set to undefined)
console.log(b);   // ReferenceError: Cannot access 'b' before initialization   (TDZ)
var a = 1;
let b = 2;

sayHi();          // works: function declarations are hoisted whole
function sayHi() { console.log('hi'); }
sayHi2();         // TypeError: sayHi2 is not a function  (var hoisted, still undefined)
var sayHi2 = function () {};</pre><p><strong>Interview tip:</strong> The TDZ is the reason <code>let</code> and <code>const</code> catch use-before-define bugs that <code>var</code> silently hides. It lasts from the start of the block until the declaration line executes.</p>`
    }
  ]
},
{
  id:"js-fn", title:"Functions & Patterns",
  questions:[
    {
      q:"What is the difference between call, apply, and bind?",
      a:`<p>All three let you explicitly set what <code>this</code> refers to inside a function. <code>call</code> invokes the function immediately with <code>this</code> and arguments passed individually; <code>apply</code> does the same but takes arguments as an array; <code>bind</code> doesn't invoke the function — it returns a new function with <code>this</code> permanently fixed, to be called later.</p>
      <pre>function greet(greeting) {
  console.log(greeting + ", " + this.name);
}
const user = { name: "Ada" };

greet.call(user, "Hello");   // Hello, Ada
greet.apply(user, ["Hi"]);   // Hi, Ada
const bound = greet.bind(user);
bound("Hey");                 // Hey, Ada</pre>
      <p><strong>Good interview signal:</strong> mentioning that arrow functions (which lexically inherit <code>this</code>) have reduced how often these show up in modern code, but <code>bind</code> is still common for passing a method as a callback without losing its intended <code>this</code>.</p>`
    },
    {
      q:"Debounce vs. throttle — what's the difference, and how would you cancel a stale request?",
      a:`<p><strong>Debounce</strong> waits until events stop for a set period before firing — good for search inputs. <strong>Throttle</strong> runs at most once per interval during a continuous stream — good for scroll/resize/mouse-move.</p>
      <pre>function debounce(fn, delay) {
  let timer;
  return (...args) => {
    clearTimeout(timer);
    timer = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), delay);
  };
}</pre>
      <p><strong>Common follow-ups</strong></p>
      <ul>
        <li><strong>How would you cancel a previous search request?</strong> Use an <code>AbortController</code> — create a new one per request and call <code>abort()</code> on the previous one before starting the next, so a slow stale response can't overwrite a newer result.</li>
        <li><strong>Can debounce be implemented with React hooks?</strong> Yes — a <code>useDebouncedValue</code> hook that updates a "debounced" state on a timer, clearing the previous timer in the effect's cleanup so only the last change survives.</li>
      </ul>`
    },
    {
      q:"What are currying and partial application, and when are they useful?",
      a:`<p class="lede"><strong>Currying</strong> turns <code>f(a, b, c)</code> into <code>f(a)(b)(c)</code>: one argument per call. <strong>Partial application</strong> fixes some arguments now and returns a function that takes the rest.</p><pre>const curry = (fn) => function curried(...args) {
  return args.length >= fn.length
    ? fn.apply(this, args)
    : (...more) => curried.apply(this, [...args, ...more]);
};

const add = (a, b, c) => a + b + c;
const cadd = curry(add);
cadd(1)(2)(3);    // 6
cadd(1, 2)(3);    // 6

// partial application with bind
const log = (level, msg) => console.log('[' + level + ']', msg);
const warn = log.bind(null, 'WARN');
warn('disk almost full');     // [WARN] disk almost full</pre><ul><li>Useful for building configured functions (a logger per level, an API client bound to a base URL, event handlers that carry an id), and for point-free composition in <code>.map</code> / <code>.filter</code> pipelines.</li><li><code>fn.length</code> counts declared parameters, so currying breaks with default or rest parameters.</li><li>A very common interview task: implement <code>curry</code> (above) and <code>compose</code> / <code>pipe</code>.</li></ul><p><strong>Interview tip:</strong> Do not oversell it: in everyday code a small closure or <code>.bind</code> is clearer than a general curry helper.</p>`
    }
  ]
},
{
  id:"js-async", title:"Async, Promises & Event Loop",
  questions:[
    {
      q:"How does the JavaScript event loop work? (call stack, microtasks, macrotasks)",
      a:`<p>JS is single-threaded: one call stack executes one thing at a time. Async work doesn't block that thread — it gets handed off and its callback is queued for later.</p>
      <div class="diagram"><svg viewBox="0 0 620 210" width="620">
    <rect x="20" y="20" width="180" height="60" rx="8" fill="var(--panel)" stroke="var(--border)" stroke-width="1.5"/>
    <text x="110" y="45" text-anchor="middle" font-family="var(--mono)" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="var(--text)">Call Stack</text>
    <text x="110" y="64" text-anchor="middle" font-family="var(--mono)" font-size="10.5" fill="var(--muted)">sync code, frame by frame</text>

    <rect x="220" y="20" width="380" height="60" rx="8" fill="var(--accent-soft)" stroke="var(--accent)" stroke-width="1.5"/>
    <text x="240" y="45" font-family="var(--mono)" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="var(--text)">Microtask queue</text>
    <text x="240" y="64" font-family="var(--mono)" font-size="10.5" fill="var(--muted)">Promises · queueMicrotask — fully drained first</text>

    <rect x="220" y="100" width="380" height="60" rx="8" fill="var(--gold-soft)" stroke="var(--gold)" stroke-width="1.5"/>
    <text x="240" y="125" font-family="var(--mono)" font-size="12" font-weight="600" fill="var(--text)">Macrotask queue</text>
    <text x="240" y="144" font-family="var(--mono)" font-size="10.5" fill="var(--muted)">setTimeout · setInterval · I/O — one per loop tick</text>

    <path d="M110 80 L110 190 L220 190" fill="none" stroke="var(--muted)" stroke-width="1.5" marker-end="url(#arrow1)"/>
    <text x="130" y="205" font-family="var(--mono)" font-size="10" fill="var(--muted)">stack empty → check queues</text>
    <defs>
      <marker id="arrow1" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="6" refY="3" orient="auto">
        <path d="M0,0 L6,3 L0,6 z" fill="var(--muted)"/>
      </marker>
    </defs>
  </svg></div>
      <ul>
        <li><strong>Call stack</strong> — runs synchronous code, frame by frame.</li>
        <li><strong>Microtask queue</strong> — Promise <code>.then/.catch/.finally</code>, <code>queueMicrotask</code>, <code>async/await</code> continuations. Drained <em>completely</em> before the next macrotask.</li>
        <li><strong>Macrotask queue</strong> — <code>setTimeout</code>, <code>setInterval</code>, I/O, UI events. One macrotask runs, then the engine checks microtasks again.</li>
      </ul>
      <p>The order that surprises people: <code>setTimeout(fn, 0)</code> always runs <em>after</em> any pending promise callbacks, no matter how "0ms" sounds.</p>
      <p><strong>Common follow-ups</strong></p>
      <ul>
        <li><strong>How can CPU-heavy work affect Node.js?</strong> Node runs JS on a single main thread, so a synchronous CPU-bound operation blocks the call stack entirely — every other request, timer, and I/O callback waits until it finishes. Offload it to <code>worker_threads</code>, a child process, or a separate service.</li>
        <li><strong>What about Node's <code>process.nextTick</code>?</strong> It runs even before other microtasks — a Node-specific queue that sits ahead of the regular microtask queue.</li>
      </ul>`
    },
    {
      q:"What problem do Promises solve, and what are their states?",
      a:`<p>A Promise wraps a value that isn't ready yet. It solves "callback hell" — deeply nested callbacks where error handling and control flow become unreadable — by letting you chain <code>.then()</code> calls and by giving async code a single, predictable shape.</p>
      <p>Three states, and the transition is one-way: <code>pending → fulfilled</code> or <code>pending → rejected</code>. Once settled, a Promise can never change state again.</p>
      <pre>fetch(url)
  .then(res => res.json())
  .then(data => process(data))
  .catch(err => handle(err));</pre>
      <p><strong>Common follow-up — what happens when an <code>async</code> function throws?</strong> An <code>async</code> function always returns a Promise, so a thrown error (or an awaited rejection) makes that returned Promise reject rather than throwing synchronously to the caller — the caller needs a <code>try/catch</code> around the <code>await</code>, or a <code>.catch</code>, or it becomes an unhandled rejection.</p>`
    },
    {
      q:"How do you coordinate several independent async operations in parallel?",
      a:`<p>The two workhorses are <code>Promise.all</code> and <code>Promise.allSettled</code>, and picking between them is really a question about failure tolerance.</p>
      <div class="diagram"><svg viewBox="0 0 600 150" width="600">
    <text x="10" y="20" font-family="var(--mono)" font-size="11.5" fill="var(--muted)">Promise.all — one fails, everything rejects</text>
    <rect x="10" y="30" width="90" height="28" rx="6" fill="var(--accent-soft)" stroke="var(--accent)"/><text x="55" y="49" text-anchor="middle" font-family="var(--mono)" font-size="11" fill="var(--text)">A ✓</text>
    <rect x="110" y="30" width="90" height="28" rx="6" fill="var(--danger)" opacity="0.25" stroke="var(--danger)"/><text x="155" y="49" text-anchor="middle" font-family="var(--mono)" font-size="11" fill="var(--text)">B ✕</text>
    <rect x="210" y="30" width="90" height="28" rx="6" fill="var(--accent-soft)" stroke="var(--accent)"/><text x="255" y="49" text-anchor="middle" font-family="var(--mono)" font-size="11" fill="var(--text)">C ✓</text>
    <text x="320" y="49" font-family="var(--mono)" font-size="13" fill="var(--danger)">→ rejects immediately</text>

    <text x="10" y="95" font-family="var(--mono)" font-size="11.5" fill="var(--muted)">Promise.allSettled — waits for all, reports each outcome</text>

    {
      q:"What are the most common Promise-chaining mistakes, and how does error propagation work through a chain?",
      a:`<p>Two mistakes come up constantly when reviewing Promise-chain code.</p>
      <p><strong>1. Forgetting to <code>return</code> the inner promise.</strong> If a <code>.then()</code> callback starts another async call but doesn't return it, the next <code>.then()</code> runs immediately with <code>undefined</code> instead of waiting for it to finish.</p>
      <pre>// ❌ Broken — doesn't wait for fetchUserPosts
fetchUserData()
  .then(user => { fetchUserPosts(user.id); })
  .then(posts => console.log(posts)); // undefined

// ✅ Fixed — returning the inner promise passes its value forward
fetchUserData()
  .then(user => fetchUserPosts(user.id))
  .then(posts => console.log(posts))
  .catch(err => console.log(err));</pre>
      <p><strong>2. Nesting instead of chaining.</strong> If you call <code>.then()</code> on the inner promise directly instead of returning it to the outer chain, any error it throws is detached from the outer <code>.catch()</code> and goes unhandled.</p>
      <pre>// ❌ Nested — errors from fetchUserPosts never reach this .catch()
fetchUserData().then(user => {
  fetchUserPosts(user.id).then(posts => console.log(posts));
}).catch(err => console.log(err));</pre>
      <p>Under the hood, when a <code>.then()</code> callback throws, the Promise implementation wraps the callback in a try/catch and immediately calls its internal reject handler with that error — which is exactly what propagates it down the chain to the nearest <code>.catch()</code>. That's also why one <code>.catch()</code> at the end of a chain can handle errors from every step before it: each rejection just keeps passing down until something handles it.</p>
      <p><strong>Common follow-ups</strong></p>
      <ul>
        <li><strong>What if a later step calls a method the earlier value doesn't have?</strong> That's just a regular runtime error (e.g. calling <code>.toFixed()</code> on a string), and it's caught and turned into a rejection exactly the same way — Promise chains don't distinguish "logic" errors from thrown exceptions.</li>
      </ul>`
    },
    {
      q:"How do you send a POST request with a JSON body using fetch?",
      a:`<p>The second argument to <code>fetch</code> is an options object — there's no separate "body" argument. Set the method, a <code>Content-Type</code> header, and serialize the body with <code>JSON.stringify</code>.</p>
<pre><code>async function createProduct(product) {
  const res = await fetch("/api/products", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify(product),
  });

  if (!res.ok) {
    throw new Error("Request failed: HTTP " + res.status);
  }
  return res.json();
}</code></pre>
<p><strong>Good interview signal:</strong> mentioning that <code>fetch</code> only rejects on a network failure (DNS error, connection refused, CORS block) — a 404 or 500 still resolves successfully, which is why <code>response.ok</code> (or checking <code>response.status</code>) has to be checked explicitly before trusting the response.</p>
<p><strong>Common follow-ups</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>How do you cancel it?</strong> Pass an <code>AbortController</code>'s <code>signal</code> in the same options object, and call <code>controller.abort()</code> — same mechanism as a GET request.</li>
<li><strong>What about FormData/file uploads?</strong> Pass a <code>FormData</code> instance as <code>body</code> directly and omit the <code>Content-Type</code> header — the browser sets the correct multipart boundary automatically; setting it manually breaks the upload.</li>
</ul>`
    },
    {
      q:"How do try / catch / finally work together, including with async/await?",
      a:`<ul>
<li><strong><code>try</code></strong> runs the code; if it throws, control jumps to <strong><code>catch</code></strong> with the error; <strong><code>finally</code></strong> runs afterwards no matter what (success, throw, or even a <code>return</code> inside try or catch).</li>
<li><strong>Use <code>finally</code> for cleanup</strong> that must always happen: closing a file or connection, hiding a spinner, releasing a lock.</li>
<li><strong>A <code>return</code> in <code>finally</code> overrides</strong> a return or throw from <code>try</code>/<code>catch</code>; avoid it.</li>
<li><strong>With <code>async/await</code>,</strong> <code>try/catch</code> catches rejections from an <em>awaited</em> promise. It does not catch errors from a promise you forgot to <code>await</code>, or from callbacks scheduled with <code>setTimeout</code>.</li>
<li><strong>Catch only what you can handle.</strong> Rethrow unknown errors, and throw <code>Error</code> objects (with a stack) rather than strings.</li>
</ul>
<pre>async function loadUser(id) {
  setLoading(true);
  try {
    const res = await fetch('/api/users/' + id);
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error('HTTP ' + res.status);   // fetch does not reject on 4xx/5xx
    return await res.json();
  } catch (err) {
    log(err);
    throw err;                                            // let the caller decide
  } finally {
    setLoading(false);                                    // always runs
  }
}</pre>
<p><strong>Gotcha:</strong> <code>return promise</code> inside <code>try</code> without <code>await</code> skips the <code>catch</code>; write <code>return await promise</code> when you want the catch to apply.</p>`
    },
    {
      q:"How do you cancel a fetch or add a timeout with AbortController?",
      a:`<pre>const ctrl = new AbortController();
const timer = setTimeout(() => ctrl.abort(), 5000);

try {
  const res = await fetch('/api/search?q=js', { signal: ctrl.signal });
  return await res.json();
} catch (err) {
  if (err.name === 'AbortError') return null;      // cancelled: not a real error
  throw err;
} finally {
  clearTimeout(timer);
}

// shortcuts
fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000) });               // timeout only
fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.any([userCtrl.signal, AbortSignal.timeout(5000)]) });   // either one</pre><ul><li><strong>Aborting rejects</strong> the promise with an <code>AbortError</code> (a <code>DOMException</code>); treat it as control flow. It cancels the browser request but the server may still process it.</li><li><strong>React search box / effect cleanup:</strong> create a controller in the effect and call <code>abort()</code> in the cleanup so a slow older response can never overwrite a newer one.</li><li>The same signal works with <code>addEventListener</code> (<code>{ signal }</code> removes the listener on abort) and many Node APIs.</li></ul><p><strong>Interview tip:</strong> This is the standard answer to "how do you avoid race conditions in typeahead?": cancel the previous request, or ignore responses that are not the latest.</p>`
    }
  ]

      q:"What's the difference between == and ===, and where does loose equality surprise people?",
      a:`<p><code>===</code> is strict equality — it compares both value and type with no coercion. <code>==</code> is loose equality — it converts the operands to a common type before comparing, which produces results many developers don't expect.</p>
      <pre>0 == false;           // true  — false coerces to 0
"" == 0;               // true  — "" coerces to 0
null == undefined;     // true  — special-cased, but null === undefined is false
"5" == 5;              // true  — string coerces to number

0 === false;           // false — different types, no coercion
"5" === 5;             // false</pre>
      <p>The practical rule: default to <code>===</code> everywhere. Reach for <code>==</code> only in the one common idiom of checking for both <code>null</code> and <code>undefined</code> at once (<code>value == null</code>), since that's the one case where the coercion is intentional and well understood.</p>
      <p><strong>Common follow-ups</strong></p>
      <ul>
        <li><strong>Is <code>NaN === NaN</code> true?</strong> No — <code>NaN</code> is the one value that isn't equal to itself under either operator. Use <code>Number.isNaN(x)</code> or <code>Object.is(x, NaN)</code> to test for it.</li>
      </ul>`

    {
      q:"Walk through chaining .map(), .filter(), and .reduce() together.",
      a:`<p>Because each of these methods returns a new value, you can chain them into a single readable pipeline instead of writing intermediate variables and loops.</p>
      <ul>
        <li><strong>map()</strong> — transforms every element, returns a new array of the <em>same length</em>.</li>
        <li><strong>filter()</strong> — keeps only elements that pass a test, returns a new array that's the same length or shorter.</li>
        <li><strong>reduce()</strong> — folds the array down to a single value (a number, object, string — whatever the accumulator ends up being).</li>
      </ul>
      <pre>const orders = [
  { product: 'Laptop',  price: 999, category: 'electronics', qty: 2 },
  { product: 'T-Shirt', price: 25,  category: 'clothing',    qty: 5 },
  { product: 'Phone',   price: 699, category: 'electronics', qty: 1 },
];

const electronicsRevenue = orders
  .map(o => ({ ...o, total: o.price * o.qty }))  // add a computed field
  .filter(o => o.category === 'electronics')       // keep only electronics
  .reduce((sum, o) => sum + o.total, 0);           // fold into one number

// (999 × 2) + (699 × 1) = 2697</pre>
      <p><strong>Common follow-ups</strong></p>
      <ul>
        <li><strong>Is chaining three methods less efficient than one loop?</strong> Yes, technically — each method does a full pass over the array. For most UI-scale data this is irrelevant; for very large arrays in a hot path, a single <code>reduce</code> (or a plain loop) that does everything in one pass avoids the extra iterations.</li>
        <li><strong>Do these mutate the original array?</strong> No — all three return new arrays/values and leave the source array untouched, which is why they're the default choice for immutable data transformations in React.</li>
      </ul>`
    },
    {
      q:"Object vs. Map — when would you reach for a Map?",
      a:`<table class="cmp">
        <tr><th></th><th>Object</th><th>Map</th></tr>
        <tr><td>Key types</td><td>String or Symbol only — a number key is silently coerced to a string</td><td>Any value, including objects and functions — never coerced</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Size</td><td>No direct property; count manually</td><td><code>map.size</code> — O(1), always accurate</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Iteration order</td><td>Integer-like keys first (ascending), then strings in insertion order — a real footgun</td><td>Always insertion order, no exceptions</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Prototype risk</td><td>Inherits from <code>Object.prototype</code> unless created with <code>Object.create(null)</code> — a key like <code>"toString"</code> can collide with an inherited method</td><td>No prototype chain to collide with</td></tr>
      </table>
      <p><strong>The practical rule:</strong> reach for <code>Map</code> whenever keys aren't known ahead of time, aren't strings, or the collection is frequently added to and removed from at runtime — a cache keyed by request objects, a memoization table keyed by function arguments. Reach for a plain object for a fixed, known shape — config, a DTO, component props — where dot-notation access and <code>JSON.stringify</code> support actually matter.</p>
      <p><strong>Common follow-up — can you use an array as a Map's key?</strong> Only by reference — two different array instances with identical contents are different keys, because Map compares object keys by identity (like <code>===</code>), not by deep equality.</p>`
    },
    {
      q:"Map vs. WeakMap — why would you choose a WeakMap?",
      a:`<p>A <code>WeakMap</code> holds its keys <strong>weakly</strong> — if nothing else in the program references a key object anymore, the garbage collector is free to reclaim it, and its entry disappears from the WeakMap automatically. A regular <code>Map</code> holds a strong reference to every key, so anything stored in a <code>Map</code> stays alive for as long as the <code>Map</code> itself does, even if nothing else needs it anymore.</p>
      <table class="cmp">
        <tr><th></th><th>Map</th><th>WeakMap</th></tr>
        <tr><td>Key types</td><td>Any value</td><td>Objects only (more recently, Symbols) — never primitives</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Garbage collection</td><td>Keys stay alive as long as the Map does</td><td>Keys can be collected once nothing else references them</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Iterable / <code>.size</code></td><td>Yes</td><td>No — by design, so you can never enumerate what's currently stored</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Use it for</td><td>A cache/registry you explicitly control the lifetime of</td><td>Metadata attached to an object you don't own the lifetime of</td></tr>
      </table>
      <p>The canonical use case: attaching private, per-instance data to DOM nodes or class instances without that attachment being the thing that keeps them alive — memoizing an expensive computation keyed by a component instance, or a library tracking "have I already initialized this element" without leaking every element it's ever touched for the life of the page.</p>
      <p><strong>Common follow-up — why can't a WeakMap be iterated?</strong> If you could list its keys, that list itself would need to hold strong references to hold them still while you iterate — which defeats the entire point of weak references. No enumeration is the trade that makes the automatic garbage collection possible.</p>`
    }
  ]
},

    {
      q:"Why use TypeScript when JavaScript already exists?",
      a:`<p>TypeScript adds static type checking, better editor tooling, safer refactoring, and clearer contracts, while compiling down to plain JavaScript. It catches many errors during development instead of at runtime — but it doesn't eliminate runtime validation, because external input (API responses, user input, database rows) is still untrusted and its types are erased entirely at runtime.</p>
      <p><strong>Good interview signal:</strong> the candidate treats TypeScript as a development-time safety net, not a runtime guarantee, and still validates external data (e.g. with Zod) rather than trusting a type annotation alone.</p>`
    },
    {
      q:"What is a tuple in TypeScript, and how is it different from an array?",
      a:`<p>A tuple is a fixed-length array type where each position has its own known type — position carries meaning, like <code>[x, y]</code> coordinates or a <code>[status, data]</code> return pair. A plain array type describes a variable-length collection where every element shares the same type, with no guarantee about length or per-position meaning.</p>
      <pre>type Result = [success: boolean, message: string];
const result: Result = [true, "Completed"];

type Range = [start: number, end?: number]; // optional trailing element
const r: Range = [10];</pre>
      <p><strong>Common follow-ups</strong></p>
      <ul>
        <li><strong>How do you model a tuple with optional elements?</strong> Mark trailing elements with <code>?</code>, same rule as optional function parameters — they must come after the required ones.</li>
        <li><strong>Tuple vs array, one more time:</strong> at runtime both are just JS arrays — the distinction (fixed length, per-position types) is purely a compile-time TypeScript concept.</li>
      </ul>`
    },
    {
      q:"What are generics, and why are they useful?",
      a:`<p>Generics let a function, class, or type defer picking a concrete type until it's actually used — a type-safe placeholder, similar in spirit to a function parameter but for types.</p>
      <pre>function firstItem<T>(list: T[]): T {
  return list[0];
}
firstItem<string>(["a","b"]); // T = string, return type is string
firstItem<number>([1,2,3]);  // T = number, return type is number</pre>
      <p>Without generics you'd either write one function per type, or use <code>any</code> and lose type safety entirely. Generics give you reusability <em>and</em> keep the type checker useful.</p>`
    },
    {
      q:"What's the difference between a type alias and an interface?",
      a:`<table class="cmp">
        <tr><th></th><th>type</th><th>interface</th></tr>
        <tr><td>Can represent</td><td>Objects, unions, intersections, primitives, tuples</td><td>Object / class shapes only</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Extending</td><td>Intersection with <code>&</code></td><td><code>extends</code> keyword</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Redeclaring the same name</td><td>Error — not allowed</td><td>Allowed, and merges (declaration merging)</td></tr>
      </table>
      <p>Rule of thumb a lot of teams use: reach for <code>interface</code> when modeling an object or class shape that might need extension later; reach for <code>type</code> when you need a union (<code>"success" | "error"</code>) or you're combining several things together.</p>
      <p><strong>Common follow-ups</strong></p>
      <ul>
        <li><strong>Can interfaces represent unions?</strong> No — an interface is a single object shape. A union needs <code>type</code> (<code>type Shape = Circle | Square</code>), though each member of that union can itself be an interface.</li>
        <li><strong>What is declaration merging?</strong> Multiple <code>interface</code> declarations with the same name automatically combine into one — handy for augmenting a library's types (e.g. adding a field to Express's <code>Request</code>) without editing the source. Type aliases don't support this.</li>
        <li><strong>When would you use an intersection type?</strong> To compose smaller type pieces together, e.g. <code>type AdminUser = User & { permissions: string[] }</code>, without needing inheritance.</li>
      </ul>`
    },
    {
      q:"Explain the Pick and Omit utility types.",
      a:`<p>Both derive a new type from an existing one without redeclaring it by hand.</p>
      <pre>interface User { id: string; name: string; email: string; password: string; }

type PublicUser = Pick<User, "id" | "name">;
// { id: string; name: string }

type SafeUser = Omit<User, "password">;
// { id: string; name: string; email: string }</pre>
      <p><code>Pick</code> is an allowlist (keep only these keys), <code>Omit</code> is a blocklist (keep everything except these keys). A good candidate should be able to say <code>Omit<T, K></code> is roughly implemented as <code>Pick<T, Exclude<keyof T, K>></code>.</p>`
    },
    {
      q:"What is the difference between unknown and any?",
      a:`<p><code>any</code> disables type checking entirely — you can do anything with an <code>any</code> value with no compiler safety net. <code>unknown</code> is the type-safe counterpart: a value can be assigned to <code>unknown</code>, but you can't use it for anything until you narrow it with a type check, so TypeScript forces you to prove what it actually is first.</p>
      <pre>function parseInput(value: unknown): string {
  if (typeof value !== "string") {
    throw new Error("Expected a string");
  }
  return value.toUpperCase(); // safe: narrowed to string
}</pre>
      <p><strong>Good interview signal:</strong> "type external data as <code>unknown</code>, then validate/narrow it with a schema library before using it as a specific type" — that's the practical pattern, not just the textbook definition.</p>`
    },
    {
      q:"What are mapped and conditional types, and what does infer do?",
      a:`<p class="lede">Mapped types build a new type by looping over the keys of another; conditional types choose a type with an <code>extends</code> test. Together they are how the built-in utility types (<code>Partial</code>, <code>Readonly</code>, <code>ReturnType</code>) are written.</p><pre>// mapped type: loop over keys
type MyPartial<T> = { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] };
type Getters<T> = { [K in keyof T as \`get\${Capitalize<string & K>}\`]: () => T[K] };   // key remapping with 'as'

// conditional type: T extends U ? X : Y
type IsString<T> = T extends string ? true : false;
type A = IsString<'x'>;      // true

// distributive over unions
type NonNull<T> = T extends null | undefined ? never : T;
type B = NonNull<string | null>;     // string

// infer: capture a type from inside a match
type ElementOf<T> = T extends (infer U)[] ? U : never;
type C = ElementOf<number[]>;        // number
type Ret<F> = F extends (...args: any[]) => infer R ? R : never;   // what ReturnType does</pre><ul><li><strong>Mapped:</strong> <code>keyof</code> gives the keys, <code>-?</code> and <code>-readonly</code> remove modifiers, <code>as</code> renames or filters keys.</li><li><strong>Conditional:</strong> when the checked type is a bare type parameter and a union is passed, it runs once per member (distribution). Wrap in <code>[T]</code> to prevent that.</li><li><strong><code>infer</code></strong> only works inside the <code>extends</code> clause of a conditional type.</li><li>Use them for library-style helpers; for application code plain interfaces and the built-in utilities are usually clearer.</li></ul><p><strong>Interview tip:</strong> Be ready to write <code>Partial</code>, <code>Pick</code> or <code>ReturnType</code> from scratch on a whiteboard.</p>`
    },
    {
      q:"Enum, union of literals, or as const object: which should you use?",
      a:`<table class="cmp"><tr><th></th><th>enum</th><th>union: 'a' | 'b'</th><th>as const object</th></tr><tr><td>Runtime code</td><td>emits an object</td><td>none (erased)</td><td>a plain object</td></tr><tr><td>Tree shaking / bundle</td><td>heavier</td><td>best</td><td>good</td></tr><tr><td>Iterate the values</td><td>yes</td><td>no</td><td>yes: <code>Object.values</code></td></tr><tr><td>Works with JSON / APIs</td><td>string enums only</td><td>natural</td><td>natural</td></tr><tr><td>Pitfalls</td><td>before TS 5.0 any numeric literal was assignable to a numeric enum (since 5.0 out-of-range literals error, but a plain <code>number</code> still is); <code>const enum</code> breaks with some compilers</td><td>no namespace for values</td><td>need a type derived from it</td></tr></table><pre>// as const object + derived union: one source of truth
export const Role = { Admin: 'admin', Editor: 'editor', Viewer: 'viewer' } as const;
export type Role = (typeof Role)[keyof typeof Role];   // 'admin' | 'editor' | 'viewer'

function can(role: Role) { return role === Role.Admin; }
Object.values(Role);            // ['admin', 'editor', 'viewer']</pre><p><strong>Interview tip:</strong> Default to a union of string literals (or the as-const pattern when you need the values at runtime). Reach for <code>enum</code> when you must match an existing codebase or need reverse lookup.</p>`
    }
  ]

  id:"ts-react", title:"TypeScript with React",
  questions:[
    {
      q:"How do you type a reusable component (like a Select) with generics?",
      a:`<p>Generics let the component's prop types — and its <code>onChange</code> callback's argument — flow from whatever type is passed to <code>options</code>, without falling back to <code>any</code>.</p>
<pre>type Option<T> = { label: string; value: T };

type SelectProps<T> = {
  options: Option<T>[];
  value: T | null;
  onChange: (v: T) => void;
};

function Select<T extends string | number>({ options, value, onChange }: SelectProps<T>) {
  return (
    <select value={value ?? ""} onChange={e => onChange(e.target.value as T)}>
      {options.map(o => <option key={String(o.value)} value={String(o.value)}>{o.label}</option>)}
    </select>
  );
}

// TypeScript infers T as "admin" | "user" from the options passed in
<Select options={[{ label: "Admin", value: "admin" }, { label: "User", value: "user" }]}
        value="admin" onChange={v => {}} /></pre>
<p>This is the same mechanism as a generic function — the type parameter is inferred at the call site — just applied to props instead of arguments.</p>`
    },
    {
      q:"How do you use discriminated unions to model component props?",
      a:`<p>A discriminated union uses one shared literal field (the "discriminant") to let TypeScript narrow which other props are valid — making invalid prop combinations a compile error instead of a runtime bug.</p>
<pre>type AlertProps =
  | { variant: "success"; message: string }
  | { variant: "error"; message: string; retryAction: () => void }
  | { variant: "loading" };

function Alert(props: AlertProps) {
  switch (props.variant) {
    case "success": return <div className="green">{props.message}</div>;
    case "error":
      return <div className="red">{props.message}<button onClick={props.retryAction}>Retry</button></div>;
    case "loading": return <div>Loading...</div>;
  }
}</pre>
<p>Passing <code>retryAction</code> to the <code>success</code> variant, or omitting it on <code>error</code>, is a type error — the compiler enforces the relationship instead of it being a runtime <code>if</code> check someone can forget.</p>`
    },
    {
      q:"What do ComponentProps, ComponentPropsWithRef, and satisfies give you?",
      a:`<p>These let you derive types instead of duplicating them by hand — useful anytime a component wraps another component or a native element.</p>
<pre>import { ComponentProps } from "react";

type InputProps = ComponentProps<"input">;          // value, onChange, placeholder, ...
type ButtonProps = ComponentProps<typeof Button>;    // props of your own component

// satisfies (TS 5+) — validates the shape without widening the inferred type
const config = { theme: "dark", size: "lg" } satisfies Record<string, string>;
// config.theme is the literal "dark", not the wider \`string\`</pre>
<p><code>ComponentProps<typeof X></code> is the idiomatic way to build a wrapper component (e.g. a styled <code>Input</code> around a native <code><input></code>) without re-declaring every prop by hand, and it stays in sync automatically if the underlying component's props change. <code>ComponentPropsWithRef</code> is the same thing but also includes the ref type.</p>`
    },
    {
      q:"React.FC vs a plain function component — which do you use, and why?",
      a:`<p>Plain function declarations are the modern default. <code>React.FC</code> used to implicitly add a <code>children</code> prop to every component — including ones that never accept children — which was removed from the official types precisely because it was too permissive.</p>
<pre>// Avoid: implicit children even when the component doesn't accept any
const Button: React.FC<{ label: string }> = ({ label }) => <button>{label}</button>;

// Prefer: explicit, and composes naturally with generics
function Button({ label }: { label: string }) {
  return <button>{label}</button>;
}

// children opted into explicitly, when actually needed
type CardProps = { title: string; children: React.ReactNode };
function Card({ title, children }: CardProps) {
  return <div><h2>{title}</h2>{children}</div>;

<p>Plain functions also make generic components straightforward (<code>function Select<T>(...)</code>) — <code>React.FC</code>'s type signature doesn't support that nearly as cleanly.</p>`
    }
  ]

{
  id:"css-box", title:"CSS: Box Model & Positioning",
  questions:[
    {
      q:"Explain the CSS box model.",
      a:`<p>Every element is a set of four nested boxes, from the inside out: <strong>content</strong> (the actual text/image), <strong>padding</strong> (space inside the border, part of the element's own background), <strong>border</strong> (drawn at the edge of the padding), and <strong>margin</strong> (transparent space outside the border, separating the element from its neighbors — and the only one of the four that can collapse with an adjacent margin).</p>
      <p>The property that changes what <code>width</code>/<code>height</code> actually measure is <code>box-sizing</code>:</p>
      <table class="cmp">
        <tr><th></th><th><code>content-box</code> (default)</th><th><code>border-box</code></th></tr>
        <tr><td><code>width</code> sets</td><td>Content only — padding and border are added on top</td><td>Content + padding + border together</td></tr>
        <tr><td>A <code>width: 200px</code> box with 20px padding renders at</td><td>240px total</td><td>200px total</td></tr>
      </table>
      <p><strong>Why this trips people up in responsive layouts:</strong> under <code>content-box</code>, adding padding to a percentage-width element makes it overflow its container, since the padding is added on top of the already-computed width. <code>border-box</code> makes width predictable regardless of padding, which is why most resets set <code>*{box-sizing:border-box}</code> globally.</p>
      <p><strong>Common follow-up — does margin ever get included?</strong> Never — margin is always outside the box the width/height math accounts for, regardless of <code>box-sizing</code>. That's also why two adjacent block elements' vertical margins can collapse into a single margin (the larger of the two), a quirk that only applies to margins, never padding or border.</p>`
    },
    {
      q:"Explain the CSS positioning schemes and when you'd use each.",
      a:`<p>The <code>position</code> property controls how an element is placed on the page, and each value changes it in a specific way.</p>
      <ul>
        <li><strong>static</strong> (the default) — normal document flow. <code>top/right/bottom/left</code> and <code>z-index</code> have no effect on it.</li>
        <li><strong>relative</strong> — stays in normal flow, but offsets are drawn relative to where the element would otherwise have been. Its original space in the layout is preserved even though it visually moves.</li>
        <li><strong>absolute</strong> — removed from normal flow entirely, positioned relative to its nearest ancestor that isn't <code>static</code> (or the viewport if none exists). Other elements lay out as if it isn't there.</li>
        <li><strong>fixed</strong> — removed from flow, positioned relative to the viewport, and stays put when the page scrolls.</li>
        <li><strong>sticky</strong> — behaves like <code>relative</code> until the element crosses a scroll threshold you define (e.g. <code>top: 0</code>), then "sticks" like <code>fixed</code> for the rest of its scroll range.</li>
      </ul>
      <p><strong>Two things interviewers check for:</strong> <code>relative</code> is not the default — <code>static</code> is — and <code>sticky</code> does not remove the element from the flow, it just changes how its offset is calculated once the threshold is crossed.</p>
      <p><strong>Common follow-ups</strong></p>
      <ul>

  id:"css-sel", title:"CSS: Selectors, Responsive & Animation",
  questions:[
    {
      q:"How do CSS combinators and specificity work when selecting elements?",
      a:`<p>Combinators describe the relationship between two selectors in the DOM tree, and mixing them up is a common source of bugs.</p>
      <table class="cmp">
        <tr><th>Combinator</th><th>Example</th><th>Matches</th></tr>
        <tr><td>Descendant</td><td><code>div ul</code></td><td>Any <code><ul></code> nested anywhere inside a <code><div></code>, at any depth</td></tr>
        <tr><td>Child</td><td><code>div > ul</code></td><td>Only a <code><ul></code> that is a direct child of a <code><div></code></td></tr>
        <tr><td>Adjacent sibling</td><td><code>div + ul</code></td><td>A <code><ul></code> that <em>immediately</em> follows a <code><div></code>, with nothing between them</td></tr>
        <tr><td>General sibling</td><td><code>div ~ ul</code></td><td>Any <code><ul></code> that follows a <code><div></code> sibling anywhere after it, not just immediately</td></tr>
      </table>
      <p>Specificity decides which rule wins when several selectors match the same element. From highest to lowest weight: inline styles, then ID selectors, then class/attribute/pseudo-class selectors, then element and pseudo-element selectors. <code>!important</code> overrides normal specificity entirely, which is exactly why it's discouraged — it breaks the predictable cascade.</p>
      <p><strong>Common follow-ups</strong></p>
      <ul>
        <li><strong>Which wins: two classes or one ID?</strong> One ID always beats any number of classes, since ID carries a higher specificity weight than class, no matter how many classes are stacked.</li>
        <li><strong>Does source order matter?</strong> Only as a tiebreaker — if two selectors have identical specificity, the one declared later in the stylesheet wins.</li>
      </ul>`
    },
    {
      q:"What principles do you follow for responsive design?",
      a:`<p>Three things working together, not one trick: relative sizing units, a layout algorithm that adapts naturally, and breakpoints for the cases that still need an explicit rule.</p>
      <table class="cmp">
        <tr><th>Unit</th><th>Relative to</th><th>Use it for</th></tr>
        <tr><td><code>rem</code></td><td>The root (<code>html</code>) font size</td><td>Spacing and font sizes — predictable everywhere, doesn't compound</td></tr>
        <tr><td><code>em</code></td><td>The current element's own font size</td><td>A value that should scale with a specific component — but compounds when nested, its main footgun</td></tr>
        <tr><td><code>%</code> / <code>vw</code>/<code>vh</code></td><td>The parent box / the viewport</td><td>Fluid widths and full-bleed sections</td></tr>
        <tr><td><code>clamp()</code></td><td>A computed range</td><td><code>font-size: clamp(1rem, 2vw + 0.5rem, 1.5rem)</code> scales fluidly between a min and max, often removing the need for a breakpoint entirely</td></tr>
      </table>
      <p><strong>Flexbox vs. Grid</strong> as the layout algorithm: Flexbox is one-dimensional (a row of nav items, centering content); Grid is two-dimensional (once you're laying out rows and columns together, like a dashboard or a card gallery) — reaching for Grid to align one row of items is over-engineering the layout.</p>
      <p><strong>Breakpoints</strong> are the fallback for cases fluid sizing can't express on its own — a genuinely different layout at small sizes (a sidebar that becomes a bottom sheet, a table that becomes stacked cards). A standard set: <code>640px</code> (mobile landscape), <code>768px</code> (tablet), <code>1024px</code> (small desktop), <code>1280px</code>+ (large desktop). <strong>Mobile-first</strong> — base styles for the smallest screen, then <code>min-width</code> media queries add complexity as space increases — keeps the cascade additive instead of fighting a desktop-first stylesheet with overrides.</p>
      <p><strong>Common follow-up — how do you handle images responsively?</strong> <code>max-width: 100%; height: auto</code> as the baseline, <code>srcset</code>/<code>sizes</code> (or <code>next/image</code>) so the browser downloads a resolution-appropriate file instead of a desktop-sized image on a phone, and <code>aspect-ratio</code> to reserve space before the image loads.</p>`
    },
    {
      q:"Why should button/UI animations use CSS transforms (like scale) instead of animating width or height?",
      a:`<p>Animating layout properties like <code>width</code>, <code>height</code>, or <code>top</code>/<code>left</code> forces the browser to redo <strong>layout</strong> (recompute geometry for the changed element and everything it affects) and <strong>paint</strong> on every frame — expensive work that runs on the main thread, competing with JavaScript and event handlers for the same time slice.</p>
      <pre><code>/* expensive — triggers layout + paint every frame */
.button:hover { width: 180px; }

/* cheap — compositor-only, skips layout and paint */
.button:hover { transform: scale(1.05); }</code></pre>
      <p><code>transform</code> (and <code>opacity</code>) skip both steps entirely. Since a transform doesn't change an element's position in the layout — it just repositions already-painted pixels — the browser can hand the whole animation to the <strong>compositor thread</strong>, a separate thread dedicated to combining already-rasterized layers. The main thread stays free, so the animation keeps running smoothly even while it's busy with something else.</p>
      <p><strong>Common follow-up — which properties are compositor-only?</strong> Essentially just <code>transform</code> and <code>opacity</code> — everything else touches layout, paint, or both. This is also why <code>will-change: transform</code> is a legitimate performance hint (it promotes the element to its own layer ahead of time), and why animating <code>box-shadow</code> is a well-known perf trap — use a pseudo-element whose <code>opacity</code> transitions a pre-rendered shadow instead.</p>`
    }
  ]
},

      a:`<p class="lede">Three puzzles that combine synchronous code, microtasks (promise callbacks, <code>queueMicrotask</code>, code after <code>await</code>) and macrotasks (<code>setTimeout</code>). Work each out before reading the answer.</p><p class="codelabel">Puzzle 1</p><pre>// Puzzle 1
console.log('A');
setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('C'));
queueMicrotask(() => console.log('D'));
console.log('E');</pre><p><strong>Prints A, E, C, D, B.</strong> Synchronous code runs first (A, E). Then the whole microtask queue drains in order (C, then D). Only then does the event loop take the next macrotask (B).</p><p class="codelabel">Puzzle 2</p><pre>// Puzzle 2

  console.log('1');
  await null;
  console.log('2');
}
run();
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('3'));
console.log('4');</pre><p><strong>Prints 1, 4, 2, 3.</strong> An async function runs synchronously until its first <code>await</code> (1). The rest of the function is queued as a microtask, <em>before</em> the <code>.then</code> registered afterwards, so 2 comes before 3.</p><p class="codelabel">Puzzle 3</p><pre>// Puzzle 3

setTimeout(() => {
  console.log('t2');
  Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('m'));
}, 0);
setTimeout(() => console.log('t3'), 0);</pre><p><strong>Prints t1, t2, m, t3.</strong> Microtasks run after <em>each</em> macrotask, not after the whole batch of timers, so <code>m</code> runs between t2 and t3.</p><div class="callout">Rule to recite: run the current synchronous code, drain all microtasks (including ones queued while draining), render if needed, take one macrotask, repeat. In Node, <code>process.nextTick</code> callbacks run before promise microtasks.</div><p><strong>Interview tip:</strong> Say the queue contents out loud step by step. Interviewers care more about the reasoning than the final string.</p>`
